title: Design a Real-Time ML Inference & Training-Data Pipeline
prompt: Design a real-time ML system for a use case like fraud detection or abuse scoring: compute streaming features from live events, serve a model with low latency on each event, log predictions and outcomes to build training data, and detect drift while safely rolling out new models via shadow and canary. Cover the online serving path, the feedback/training-data loop, and monitoring.
blurb: The closed-loop real-time ML system — streaming features, low-latency serving, drift detection, and shadow/canary rollout.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (compute features, score events, log outcomes, retrain, roll out) from non-functional (scoring latency, throughput, freshness, safe deploys).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about event QPS, per-event latency budget, label availability/delay, freshness of streaming features, and consequences of false positives/negatives.

rubric.label: Back-of-envelope estimations
rubric.description: Estimates event QPS, streaming feature state size, model inference latency budget, prediction-log volume, and label delay window.

rubric.label: Streaming feature computation
rubric.description: Windowed aggregations over event streams, stateful stream processing, exactly-once vs at-least-once, and freshness of real-time features.

rubric.label: Model serving
rubric.description: Low-latency online scoring, feature fetch + on-event features, model registry, versioning, and fallback on model/feature failure.

rubric.label: Training-data / feedback loop
rubric.description: Logging predictions with feature snapshots, joining delayed labels/outcomes, point-in-time correctness, and closing the loop for retraining.

rubric.label: Drift detection
rubric.description: Monitoring feature/prediction/label distribution shift and performance decay; triggering retraining or alerts.

rubric.label: Shadow & canary rollout
rubric.description: Shadow (score without acting) to compare a new model, canary/gradual rollout with guardrail metrics, and automatic rollback.

rubric.label: Monitoring & observability
rubric.description: Latency/error SLOs, feature freshness, model performance metrics, drift alerts, and prediction/outcome dashboards.

rubric.label: ML system specifics
rubric.description: Training/serving skew avoidance, label delay handling, retraining cadence, offline eval before rollout, and reproducibility.

rubric.label: Reliability
rubric.description: Graceful degradation when a feature source or model is unavailable, backpressure, and idempotent event processing.

rubric.label: Scaling
rubric.description: Partitioning the stream, scaling stateful operators, sharding the online store, and horizontally scaling serving.

functional_requirements: Compute streaming features from live events (windowed aggregates, counts, velocities)
Score each event with a model in real time and return a decision
Log predictions with the exact features used
Join delayed ground-truth outcomes to build training labels
Retrain and safely roll out new models (shadow → canary → full)
nonfunctional_requirements: No training/serving skew; reproducible training data
Safe deploys with automatic rollback on guardrail breach
clarifying_questions: What's the event QPS and the per-event latency budget?
How and when do ground-truth labels arrive (delay, coverage)?
How fresh must streaming features be, and over what windows?
What's the cost of a false positive vs false negative?
Is the decision synchronous (blocks the event) or can it be async?
How often do we retrain, and can we shadow/canary safely?
qualifying_questions: Do we need exactly-once feature semantics or is at-least-once acceptable?
Is there a human-in-the-loop review for high-risk decisions?

estimations.traffic: ~30k events/s peak; each event = feature fetch/compute + 1 model score
estimations.feature_state: Windowed aggregates per entity (user/card/device) over minutes-to-days → millions of keys x several counters kept in the stream processor's state or an online store
estimations.latency_budget: ~50ms: feature fetch ~5-15ms + on-event compute + model inference ~5-20ms
estimations.prediction_log: 30k/s x (features + score) ≈ large; write to a log/warehouse for the training loop
estimations.label_delay: Fraud chargebacks may arrive days later → training joins must handle a long, sparse label window

core_components: Stream processor for windowed/stateful features (e.g. Flink)
Online feature store (latest streaming feature values)
data_model: predictions(pred_id, event_id, model_version, features_snapshot, score, decision, ts)
reference.high_level_design: Events land on a partitioned stream. A stateful stream processor computes windowed features per entity (counts, velocities, aggregates over sliding windows) and writes latest values to an online feature store. On each event needing a decision, the serving service fetches streaming features + computes any on-event features, scores with the current production model, returns a decision synchronously, and logs the exact feature snapshot + score + model version. Ground-truth outcomes arrive later (seconds to days) and are joined to the logged predictions by event_id to form point-in-time-correct training examples — closing the loop. Offline, models retrain on this data and are validated. New models deploy first in shadow mode (scored on live traffic but their decisions aren't acted on, compared against prod), then canary on a small traffic slice with guardrail metrics, then full rollout — with automatic rollback if guardrails breach. A monitor tracks feature/prediction/label drift and model performance to trigger retraining.

deep_dives.probe: You need per-entity velocity over the last 1m/1h/24h with sub-second freshness. How do you compute sliding-window aggregates in a stream processor, manage that state, and handle late/out-of-order events?
Labels arrive days after the prediction. How do you build a leak-free training set — snapshot features at scoring time, join delayed labels, and ensure the features match exactly what serving used?

Your model silently degrades. What do you monitor — input feature drift, prediction drift, or actual performance once labels arrive — and how do you distinguish drift from noise and decide to retrain?
Walk me through safely deploying a new model. What's the difference between shadow and canary, which guardrail metrics gate promotion, and how does automatic rollback work?
A feature source times out mid-request. What do you do — default/impute the feature, fall back to a simpler model, or fail open/closed? How does that depend on false-positive/negative cost?
How do you guarantee the streaming feature value used online is exactly what you train on offline (no skew), given late events and reprocessing?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions feature store or online store or source data or database
followup_bank.question: When upstream/source data changes or a late event arrives, how do the online streaming features stay in sync and consistent with what you'll train on — CDC/stream reprocessing, watermarks, event-time joins? What's the staleness bound?
You cache features or model outputs per entity. What's the eviction/TTL policy, and how do you invalidate when a new event updates the entity's windowed features so you don't score on stale state?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions kafka or stream or flink or queue
followup_bank.question: How do you handle late/out-of-order events and exactly-once vs at-least-once so features and training labels stay correct?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions model or retrain or deploy
followup_bank.question: How do you detect drift and decide when to retrain, and how do shadow/canary guardrails gate the rollout with automatic rollback?

scaling: Partition the stream by entity key so stateful features scale horizontally
Scale stream-processor operators; use RocksDB-backed keyed state + checkpoints
Shard the online feature store; cache hot entities
Horizontally scale stateless serving; batch where latency allows
Separate the high-volume prediction-log write path from serving
bottlenecks: Stateful stream-processor state size and checkpoint cost
Feature fetch latency inside the scoring budget
Label delay makes performance monitoring lag reality
Training/serving skew from late events and reprocessing
tradeoffs: Sync scoring (blocks event, simplest) vs async (throughput, complexity)
Exactly-once (correct, costly) vs at-least-once (cheaper, dedupe needed)
Fresh streaming features (state/compute cost) vs batch approximations
Fail-open (availability) vs fail-closed (safety) on feature/model failure
Fast rollout vs long shadow/canary soak for safety
alternative_solutions: Batch scoring on a schedule (simpler, too slow for fraud)
Micro-batch (e.g. Spark Structured Streaming) instead of true streaming
Precompute features nightly + only on-event features online (staleness tradeoff)
observability: Scoring latency and error SLOs; feature-fetch latency
Feature/prediction drift metrics; performance metrics once labels land
Shadow-vs-prod agreement and canary guardrail dashboards
security: PII minimization in features and prediction logs
Access control on features, models, and decisions
Audit trail of decisions and model versions for disputes/compliance
Abuse-resistance so adversaries can't reverse-engineer thresholds
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer designs a closed loop: a partitioned event stream feeding a stateful stream processor that computes windowed per-entity features (with watermarks for late/out-of-order events) into an online store; a low-latency serving path that fetches features, scores with a versioned model, returns a decision, and logs the exact feature snapshot + score + model version. It closes the loop by joining delayed ground-truth labels back to those logged predictions to build point-in-time-correct, skew-free training data, then retrains and rolls out via shadow (compare on live traffic without acting), canary (small slice with guardrail metrics), and automatic rollback. It monitors input/prediction/performance drift to trigger retraining, handles feature/model failure with an explicit fail-open/closed decision tied to error cost, and calls out stream-state size, feature-fetch latency, label delay, and training/serving skew from reprocessing as the key hazards.

interviewer_notes: This question tests whether a candidate can reason about a full closed-loop ML system, not just a model endpoint. The strongest signals: (1) the training-data loop — snapshotting features at scoring time and joining delayed labels point-in-time-correctly; if they log only the score and not the features, or ignore label delay, that's a major gap. (2) drift detection — push them to distinguish feature drift, prediction drift, and true performance decay (which lags because labels are late). (3) shadow vs canary — many conflate them; make them articulate shadow = score-but-don't-act comparison vs canary = small live slice with guardrails and rollback. Use the streaming-sync follow-up (late events, watermarks, CDC/reprocessing keeping features consistent with training) and the cache-invalidation follow-up as interrupts. Probe the fail-open vs fail-closed decision on feature timeout and tie it to false-positive/negative cost. Reserve time for stateful stream processing (windowed aggregates, late data) — this is where senior candidates show depth.
